content: The guideline development process involved a diverse group of experts and representatives from various institutions worldwide. These included prominent figures such as Peter Fonjungo from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Carlo Giaquinto from the University of Padova in Italy, Diane Havlir from the University of California at San Francisco, and Charles Holmes from the Center for Infectious Disease Research in Zambia. Other contributors included John Idoko from Nigeria’s National Agency for the Control of AIDS, Andreas Jahn from ITECH in Malawi, and Quarraisha Abdool Karim from CAPRISA in South Africa. Additional contributors included Nagalingeswaran Kumarasamy from YRG CARE in India, Karine Lacombe from Saint Antoine Hospital in Paris, and Loyce Maturu from Africaid in Zimbabwe. Dorothy Mbori-Ngacha from UNICEF South Africa, Lynne Mofenson from the Elizabeth Glaser Pediatric AIDS Foundation, and Angela Mushavi from Zimbabwe’s Ministry of Health and Child Care also played key roles. Landon Myer from the University of Cape Town, Angelina Namiba from Positively UK, and Shinichi Oka from the National Center for Global Health and Medicine in Tokyo were also involved. Ryan Phelps from the United States Agency for International Development, Andrew Prendergast from the Medical Research Council in the United Kingdom, and Elliot Raizes from the CDC contributed as well. George Siberry from the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, Annette Sohn from TREAT Asia in Thailand, and Bukiki Sylvere from the International Treatment Preparedness Coalition in Côte d’Ivoire were among the contributors. Denis Tindyebwa from the African Network for Care of Children Affected by HIV/AIDS in Uganda, Francois Venter from the University of Witwatersrand in South Africa, and Heather Watts from the Office of the Global AIDS Coordinator in the U.S. Department of State also participated. Benjamin Young from the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care in the USA, Oleg Yurin from the Federal AIDS Centre in Russia, and Fujie Zhang from the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention were also part of the team. The external review group included Ruth Birgin from the International Network of People who Use Drugs in Australia, Olga Denisiuk from the International HIV Alliance in Ukraine, and Agata Dziuban from Jagiellonian University in Poland. Robert Grant and Jae Sevelius from the University of California, San Francisco, Praphan Phanuphak from the Thai Red Cross, Nathan Shaffer from WHO’s Department of HIV/AIDS, and Joseph Tucker from the UNC Project in China also contributed to the review process. Representatives from United Nations agencies and other partners included Martin Auton from the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria in Switzerland, Smiljka De Lussigny from UNITAID in Switzerland, Peter Godfrey Fausett from UNAIDS in Switzerland, Chewe Luo from UNICEF in Kenya, Atieno Ojoo from UNICEF, and Carlos Passerelli from UNAIDS in Switzerland. Funding for the development of this guideline was provided by grants from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the United States Agency for International Development, the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR). In 2013, the World Health Organization (WHO) published its first consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs for HIV treatment and prevention across all age groups and populations. A comprehensive revision of these guidelines, based on new scientific evidence and lessons learned from implementation, was undertaken in 2015. This early-release guideline introduces two key recommendations developed during the 2015 revision process. The first recommendation is that antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be initiated in all individuals living with HIV, regardless of their CD4 cell count. This recommendation is supported by evidence from clinical trials and observational studies demonstrating that earlier initiation of ART leads to better clinical outcomes compared to delayed treatment. The second recommendation is the use of daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) as a prevention option for individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection. This recommendation is based on clinical trial results confirming the efficacy of the ARV drug tenofovir, either alone or in combination with emtricitabine, in preventing HIV acquisition across various settings and populations. These recommendations are being released early due to their potential to significantly reduce the number of new HIV infections and HIV-related deaths, thereby having a profound impact on global public health. By publishing these recommendations promptly, WHO aims to assist countries in anticipating their implications and initiating the necessary dialogue to ensure that national HIV prevention and treatment standards align with the latest scientific advancements. The primary audience for this guideline includes national HIV program managers, who will be responsible for adapting the new recommendations at the country level. The guideline will also be of interest to a wide range of stakeholders, including national tuberculosis program managers, civil society organizations, and both domestic and international funders of HIV programs. The recommendations in this guideline will be incorporated into the revised consolidated guidelines on the use of ARV drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, which WHO plans to publish in 2016. The full update will include comprehensive clinical recommendations along with revised operational and service delivery guidance to support implementation. The ambitious UNAIDS Fast-Track targets for 2020, including the 90–90–90 targets, require countries to accelerate their HIV responses. These targets aim for 90% of people living with HIV to know their status, 90% of those diagnosed to access ART, and 90% of those on treatment to achieve viral suppression. Achieving these goals will necessitate greater efforts to ensure that key and vulnerable populations, as well as adolescents, have access to essential HIV treatment and prevention services. The implementation of these recommendations will contribute to achieving these targets and ultimately ending the AIDS epidemic as a major public health threat by 2030.
